title: Opposition: one tempo between a win and a draw (part 3 of 3)
outcomes: Takes the opposition in a king-and-pawn ending when it is the move that wins, and explains in words why the side not to move holds it
Predicts win or draw for king and pawn against king, and sees that one tempo, a spare pawn step or one king square can flip it
Names the cases where 'the side not to move wins' fails: a king level with the pawn, an edge pawn, a distant defender, and the pawn on its sixth rank
Links the opposition to key squares and says what the opposition is for
Teaches the idea to a beginner with an example, a condition and a warning

steps.text: Part 3 of 3: Opposition: one tempo between a win and a draw. This part covers Mixed test and real endings; Say it back. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Mixed test.** From here nothing is labelled, and some positions are not about the opposition at all. For each one ask: whose move is it, where is each king compared with the pawn and its key squares, and is the pawn on the edge of the board? Sometimes the answer is that the move does not matter.

steps.prompt: Before each prediction: did you ask who was to move, or where each king stood? Which of the two did you check first, and which did you forget?

steps.text: **Four real endings.** They come from game records in the Lichess broadcast archive (moves are public facts; the comments are ours). In the first, a 2561-rated player had only king and pawn left against a 2563-rated opponent. Before you see the moves, notice that White is to move and that no king faces the other.

steps.caption: Kantor v Yoo, Saint Louis, 8 Nov 2022. White to move. Five king moves win; both pawn pushes and two king retreats only draw. The game continued as shown.

line.say: White brought the king forward onto Black's file. Several king moves win here, so no exact opposition is needed.
Black stepped aside.
White's king kept advancing past the pawn's file.
Black fell back.
White's king reached the sixth rank. The game record gives White the win a few moves later.

claims.statement: With White to move the tablebase result for White is a win.
The pawn step f3 only draws.
The pawn step f4 only draws.

steps.prompt: [H] Write a guess: why would both pawn pushes only draw here, while five king moves win? Think about what the black king can do once the pawn has moved.

steps.text: **A guess, labelled.** [H] After a pawn push the black king, still free to roam, may reach the squares in front of the pawn before the white king has made room. Capablanca's practical advice for these endings was to walk the king forward and push the pawn mainly to keep it safe. The tablebase confirms the result on the board; it does not prove our explanation.

steps.prompt: Teach it to an imagined beginner who has just learned how the pieces move. Write the idea, when it works, one example, and one warning, in your own words.

fields.label: When it works, and when it fails:
One example a beginner could set up on a board:

steps.caption: Keymer v Smeets, Schachbundesliga (header date 8 Dec 2019). Black to move, and every Black move loses. In the game Black played Ke8 and White pushed the pawn.

line.say: Black takes the square in front of the pawn.
The pawn steps ahead, guarded by the king. The record ends here with a win for White.

claims.statement: With Black to move the tablebase result for Black is a loss.

steps.caption: The same placement with White to move. Now the pawn push only draws and the king step wins. Here the move decides only which piece advances.

line.say: The king steps beside the pawn's path and takes away the black king's best squares.
Black runs towards the pawn's rear.
Now the pawn goes, guarded by its king.
Black attacks the pawn.
The pawn becomes a queen, guarded by the king.

claims.statement: With White to move the tablebase result for White is a win.

steps.caption: Stefansson v Bjornsson, Reykjavik Open, 3 Apr 2023 (ratings 2510 and 2310 in the record). Black's king is far from the pawn, and Black to move loses. The game ended a few moves later.

line.say: Black looks for a way back.
White's king goes forward, not the pawn.
Black keeps walking.
White's king reaches the sixth rank.
Black runs out of squares.
White's king takes the squares in front of the pawn's path. The record gives White the win.

claims.statement: With Black to move the tablebase result for Black is a loss.

steps.caption: Mkrtchian v Harika, FIDE Online Olympiad play-off, 28 Aug 2020 (ratings 2388 and 2515 in the record). Colours reversed: Black has the pawn. Black to move wins, and the game continued as shown.

line.say: Black's king steps to the side of White's king, keeping ahead of the pawn.
White's king advances.
Now the pawn goes, guarded by the king from behind.
White tries to run towards the pawn's path.
The pawn advances again.
White's king keeps coming.
Black's king steps in front of the pawn's path to guard it.
White keeps going, but is too far behind.

claims.statement: With Black to move the tablebase result for Black is a win.
The pawn step f6 also wins.
The pawn step f5 only draws here.

steps.text: **What to remember.** The opposition is a position plus a turn: the kings face with one square between and the other side must move. It wins when the attacking king is ahead of the pawn and the defender is near. It fails for a king level with the pawn, an edge pawn or a faraway defender, and on the sixth rank it can reverse. Always ask whose move it is.

**Self-check before you write.** Did you say when the opposition works? Did you say when it fails and name at least one failing look-alike? Did you give an example a beginner could set up on a board? Did you name one mistake, such as pushing the pawn too early? The app does not grade this; you are the judge.
